title: India Just Gave Its First Space Funding to Private Startups. A Rocket Engine, an AI Satellite Brain, and a Star Tracker Made the Cut.
excerpt: IN-SPACe picks three companies under its ₹500 crore Technology Adoption Fund — the first time the Indian government has directly invested in non-governmental space ventures.
body:
India's space regulator has picked the first three private startups to receive government funding for developing critical space technologies — a reusable rocket engine, an AI-powered Earth observation platform, and an indigenous satellite navigation system. The move marks a new chapter in a sector that, until recently, belonged almost entirely to the state-run Indian Space Research Organisation.

The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre, known as IN-SPACe, announced the selections under its Technology Adoption Fund, a ₹500 crore initiative launched in February 2026 to help early-stage space companies bridge the gap between prototyping and commercial viability. Each project can receive up to ₹25 crore, with the government covering 60 per cent of costs.

## The Three Companies

Bengaluru-based **Astrobase Space Technologies**, founded by former ISRO propulsion engineer Devakumar Thammisetty and CoinDCX co-founder Neeraj Khandelwal, will develop an 800-kilonewton closed-cycle liquid rocket engine fuelled by liquid oxygen and liquefied natural gas. The engine is designed to be reusable and powerful enough to launch medium- and heavy-lift vehicles — capabilities that currently sit with ISRO alone in India.

**SatSure Analytics India**, also headquartered in Bengaluru, secured a ₹24.6 crore grant to build Dhaarini, a large Earth observation foundation model. The AI platform will convert satellite and drone imagery into actionable intelligence for agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, and disaster response. Co-founder and CTO Rashmit Singh Sukhmani said Dhaarini would be tailored to India's geography, climate dynamics, and agricultural diversity — areas where global models often struggle with local conditions.

Hyderabad-based **TM2SPACE Technologies** will develop AI-enabled star tracker systems for CubeSats and larger satellites, improving the pointing accuracy needed for high-resolution imaging and communications missions.

## A Sector That Belonged to ISRO Alone

India opened its space sector to private participation in 2020 with the creation of IN-SPACe, but funding has been the persistent bottleneck. Most of India's 200-odd space startups have relied on venture capital, corporate grants, or foreign investors. The Technology Adoption Fund is the first time the Indian government has directly invested in non-governmental space companies.

"With this fund, our vision is to bridge the critical gap between early-stage development and commercial success," said Dr Pawan Goenka, IN-SPACe chairman. "By offering this financial support, we are empowering the private sector to work on cutting-edge space technologies."

The startups were shortlisted through a multi-stage evaluation involving experts from ISRO, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, the Department of Science and Technology, and academia. The fund targets technologies where India depends on imports or lacks sovereign capability.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

India's private space sector has deep connections to its overseas talent pool. Several founders have returned from positions at NASA, SpaceX, and European space agencies. SatSure's founding team includes alumni of IITs and international aerospace programmes. Astrobase's co-founder built propulsion systems at ISRO before launching the company.

For NRI investors and technologists watching India's space ambitions, the government's willingness to put public money behind private companies signals that the sector has moved beyond aspiration. India has committed a ₹1,000 crore fund to help space startups scale up, and the Technology Adoption Fund now provides a structured pathway for commercialising technologies that were previously developed only inside ISRO's own laboratories.

The development also coincides with SatSure's participation in India's programme to build a commercial satellite constellation — a project that could eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink and OneWeb in the low-Earth orbit communications market.
